outputs.L2:
“Are the fields still being worked by my team—the horses I once guided while listening to the tack ring, back when I was alive?”

“Yes. The horses still stamp across the earth, and the harness continues to chime. Nothing has altered, even though you now rest beneath the soil you formerly turned.”

“Do the boys still play football beside the river, running after the leather ball now that I can no longer rise?”

“Yes. The ball still races through the air, and the players give everything they have. The posts remain upright, and the goalkeeper stands ready to defend them.”

“And what of the woman I loved and hated to leave? Is she happy? Has she stopped crying when she goes to bed each evening?”

“Yes. She settles down without sorrow now. She no longer lies awake in tears; she is perfectly satisfied. Quiet yourself, my boy, and return to sleep.”

“Is my friend doing well while I waste away in death? Has he discovered a more comfortable bed than the one I occupy?”

“Yes, lad. I rest comfortably—in the sort of bed any young man would gladly choose. I bring comfort to the sweetheart of someone who has died, but do not ask me which dead man she belonged to.”
outputs.L3:
In a conversation from beyond the grave, a dead man asks his surviving friend whether his old team of horses is still ploughing the fields he once worked. His friend assures him that farm life continues exactly as before: the horses pull their harnesses, and the land is cultivated despite his absence. The dead man then asks whether the young men of the village still play football by the river. Again, he learns that life has carried on without him, with the players competing as energetically as ever.

Turning to more personal concerns, the dead man wonders whether his former sweetheart is still grieving at his death. His friend replies that she no longer weeps and now appears content. Finally, the friend admits, though indirectly, that he has taken the dead man’s place in her affections and is now sleeping with her. He claims to be comforting her well, but pointedly warns the dead man not to ask whose bed he shares. This final revelation gives the exchange a bitterly ironic ending: while the dead man remains preoccupied with the life he lost, both the community and the woman he loved have moved on without him.
outputs.L4:
In A. E. Housman’s poem **“Is My Team Ploughing,”** a dead young man questions a living friend about the world he has left behind. He first asks whether his horses are still ploughing the land and whether the boys are still playing football by the river. His friend replies that both work and play continue just as they did before his death. The horses still pull the plough, the fields are cultivated, and the young men carry on with their games. These answers emphasize that nature and everyday life remain largely unchanged by an individual’s death.

The dead man then turns to more personal concerns. He asks whether his former sweetheart still mourns for him and whether his friend is healthy and happy. The living man reassures him that the girl is well, but his evasive language gradually reveals an uncomfortable truth: he himself has taken the dead man’s place beside her. Although he claims to be a loyal friend, he now shares the sweetheart’s bed and comforts her in the dead man’s absence.

The poem therefore moves from ordinary continuity to intimate betrayal. Its alternating dialogue creates suspense, as the living friend avoids speaking openly until the final lines expose what has happened. Life continues after death, but it does so partly by replacing those who have died. Work, play, love, and friendship survive, yet individual people prove disturbingly replaceable. Housman’s dark irony lies in the contrast between the friend’s apparent reassurance and the painful truth behind it: the dead man has not only been forgotten by the larger world but has also been displaced in his most personal relationships.
outputs.L5:
**That, And, When**

“That” points to something—a memory, an idea, a distant place. “And” connects one thing to another, allowing thoughts and stories to grow. “When” asks about time, inviting us to look backward or imagine what lies ahead.

Together, these simple words shape the way we speak and think. We remember **that** moment, connect it to another with **and**, and wonder **when** everything began—or when it might change.

counterfactuals.output:
### “Is My Team Ploughing?”
*By A. E. Housman*

“Is my team ploughing,  
That I was used to drive  
And hear the harness jingle  
When I was man alive?”

Ay, the horses trample,  
The harness jingles now;  
No change though you lie under  
The land you used to plough.

“Is football playing  
Along the river shore,  
With lads to chase the leather,  
Now I stand up no more?”

Ay, the ball is flying,  
The lads play heart and soul;  
The goal stands up, the keeper  
Stands up to keep the goal.

“Is my girl happy,  
That I thought hard to leave,  
And has she tired of weeping  
As she lies down at eve?”

Ay, she lies down lightly,  
She lies not down to weep:  
Your girl is well contented.  
Be still, my lad, and sleep.

“Is my friend hearty,  
Now I am thin and pine,  
And has he found to sleep in  
A better bed than mine?”

Yes, lad, I lie easy,  
I lie as lads would choose;  
I cheer a dead man’s sweetheart,  
Never ask me whose.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1
